notes.text: For more than 8, shape two loaves side by side on the sheet pan, with a hand's width between them, and check each one with the thermometer.

move.title: Holds together, cooked through
move.body: A binder is what holds ground meat together so it slices instead of crumbling. Today you'll soak oats in milk, mix them with egg and beef, shape a loaf, and bake it with a sweet tomato glaze. The outside browns long before the middle is safe, so only the thermometer can tell you it's done: 160°F in the center.

why.title: Oats and egg hold it together
why.body: Oats soaked in milk turn soft and sticky. They hold on to the beef's juices as it cooks, so the loaf stays moist. The egg sets in the oven like glue, holding every crumb in place. Without them, meatloaf falls apart into a pan of crumbly beef.

why.title: Mix gently
why.body: Squeezing and kneading ground beef packs it tight, and a tight loaf bakes up tough and dense. Mix with your fingers spread open, lifting and turning, just until you can't see streaks of oats or egg. Then stop.

why.title: The middle cooks last
why.body: Oven heat soaks into the loaf from the outside in. The edges are brown and sizzling long before the very center gets hot. Color can't tell you when ground beef is safe, because the inside can turn brown before it's hot enough. The thermometer, in the thickest part, is the only test: 160°F.

why.title: Glaze twice
why.body: The glaze has sugar in it, and sugar burns if it bakes too long. Half goes on at the start to soak in, and the rest goes on near the end so it turns shiny and sticky instead of black.

why.title: Let it rest
why.body: A loaf straight from the oven is so soft that it crumbles under the knife, and its juices run out onto the board. Ten minutes of rest lets it firm up and the juices settle back in, so every slice holds together. It keeps cooking a little while it rests, too.

wrong.sign: The loaf crumbles when you slice it
wrong.fix: Let it rest longer before slicing, and use a sawing motion with the knife. Next time, make sure the oats soak until soft before the beef goes in.

wrong.sign: The outside is brown but the middle reads under 160°F
wrong.fix: Keep baking and check every 5 minutes. A thick middle is always the last part to get hot.
Lay a loose sheet of foil over the top for the rest of the baking time.

wrong.sign: The loaf spread flat on the pan
wrong.fix: It still tastes the same. Next time, shape it taller and narrower, and press the sides firm.

quiz.q: How do you know the meatloaf is safe to eat?
choices: The thermometer reads 160°F in the center
It has baked for one hour
quiz.explain: Color and time can fool you. Only the temperature in the thickest part tells you ground beef is safe.

quiz.q: Why do oats go into meatloaf?
choices: They hold the juices and help the loaf hold together
quiz.explain: Soaked oats are a binder: they keep the loaf moist and help it slice in clean pieces.

steps.text: Put a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 375°F. Line the sheet pan with foil.
steps.tip: Foil makes cleanup easy: the drippings stay on it, not the pan.

steps.text: In the large bowl, stir the oats and milk together. Leave them to soak while you cut the onion.
steps.look: The oats are soft and have soaked up most of the milk.

steps.text: Cut the onion in half through the root and peel it. Dice it small, smaller than a pea, so it melts into the loaf.
steps.tip: Lay each half flat side down so it can't roll, and keep your other hand in a claw.

steps.text: Crack the {n:egg} eggs into the small bowl, then tip them into the oats. Add the onion, the loaf's ketchup, the garlic powder, thyme, {qty:salt} salt, and {qty:black-pepper} pepper. Stir with the fork until it's smooth.
steps.tip: Cracking into a small bowl first means you can fish out any shell before it's lost in the mix.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter where the eggs were.

Add the beef to the bowl. Mix it in with your fingers spread open, lifting and turning, just until there are no streaks of oats. Tip it onto the lined pan and shape it into a loaf about 9 inches long, 5 inches wide, and 2 inches tall.
steps.tip: Wet your hands with cold water before shaping, and the beef won't stick to them.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap. Put the bowl and fork in the sink, and wipe anything the raw beef or its package touched.
steps.tip: Raw beef can carry germs. Wash before you touch the glaze or anything else.

steps.text: In the clean small bowl, stir together the glaze's ketchup, the brown sugar, and the mustard. Spoon half of it over the top of the loaf and spread it with the back of the spoon. Put that spoon in the sink.
steps.tip: The spoon touched the raw loaf, so it doesn't go back in the glaze. You'll use a clean one for the second coat.

steps.text: Put the pan in the oven and bake.
steps.tip: Wash up the bowls while it bakes.

steps.text: With oven mitts on, pull the pan out onto the stovetop. Spoon the rest of the glaze over the top with a clean spoon, then put it back in the oven.
steps.look: The glaze is shiny and sticky, and the edges of the loaf are browned and sizzling.

steps.text: With oven mitts on, pull the pan out. Slide the thermometer into the very middle of the loaf, from the end, so the tip is in the center. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, bake 5 more minutes and check again.
Turn off the oven. Leave the loaf on the pan to rest.
Lift the loaf onto the cutting board with the spatula. Slice it about 1 inch thick with a gentle sawing motion, and serve.
steps.tip: Store leftovers covered in the fridge. The USDA guideline is 3 to 4 days. Reheat slices until they reach 165°F.

move.body: A binder is what holds ground meat together so it slices instead of crumbling. Today you'll soak oats in milk, mix them with egg and ground turkey, shape a loaf, and bake it with a sweet tomato glaze. The outside browns long before the middle is safe, so only the thermometer can tell you it's done: 165°F in the center, because turkey is poultry.

middle-last.title: The middle cooks last
middle-last.body: Oven heat soaks into the loaf from the outside in. The edges are brown and sizzling long before the very center gets hot. Color can't tell you when ground turkey is safe. The thermometer, in the thickest part, is the only test, and turkey is poultry, so it's 165°F, not the 160°F for beef.

add.title: Poultry is 165°F
add.body: Every kind of poultry, ground or whole, cooks to 165°F. Ground beef is safe at 160°F. Mixing them up is the most common thermometer mistake, so check the chart: the meat decides the number, not the recipe.

wrong.sign: The loaf crumbles when you slice it
wrong.fix: Let it rest longer before slicing, and use a sawing motion with the knife. Next time, make sure the oats soak until soft before the turkey goes in.

wrong.sign: The outside is brown but the middle reads under 165°F
wrong.fix: Keep baking and check every 5 minutes. A thick middle is always the last part to get hot.
Lay a loose sheet of foil over the top for the rest of the baking time.
Turkey is lean, so it dries out if it bakes long past 165°F. Start checking a little early next time.

quiz.q: What temperature does turkey meatloaf need to reach?
quiz.explain: Turkey is poultry, and all poultry cooks to 165°F. Ground beef is 160°F.

quiz.q: Why do oats go into meatloaf?
choices: They hold the juices and help the loaf hold together
quiz.explain: Soaked oats are a binder: they keep the loaf moist and help it slice in clean pieces.

mix-shape.text: Add the turkey to the bowl. Mix it in with your fingers spread open, lifting and turning, just until there are no streaks of oats. Tip it onto the lined pan and shape it into a loaf about 9 inches long, 5 inches wide, and 2 inches tall.
mix-shape.tip: Turkey is stickier than beef. Wet your hands with cold water before shaping.

wash-beef.text: Wash your hands with soap. Put the bowl and fork in the sink, and wipe anything the raw turkey or its package touched.
wash-beef.tip: Raw poultry can carry germs. Wash before you touch the glaze or anything else.

check.text: With oven mitts on, pull the pan out. Slide the thermometer into the very middle of the loaf, from the end, so the tip is in the center. Turkey needs to read at least 165°F, hotter than beef. If it doesn't, bake 5 more minutes and check again.
